[SYSTEM]
You are a senior absolute oral bioavailability F-threshold reasoning model. Integrate evidence direction and transferability without converting uncertainty into a negative outcome. 

L6 adds hepatic-clearance and metabolic-stability experiments. Use them as mechanistic evidence for systemic presystemic loss while preserving species, assay system, and measurement direction; they are not direct oral- bioavailability results or extra gold votes.

This is progressive assay-transfer reasoning. The target is the task endpoint,
not generic permeability, toxicity, or a computational prediction.

Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.
Missing source values are omitted; do not assume a hidden canonicalized value.


L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference
context's accepted oral-bioavailability outcome. Give greatest endpoint weight
to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-
reference exposure; interpret AUC, Cmax, dose, route, formulation, species, and
sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.
Use these usually more indirect records to clarify absorption, exposure,
formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome
may not generalize. Permeability, solubility, or mechanism alone is not a direct
oral-bioavailability outcome.


First determine what every measurement says about its reference molecule. L2
records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.

claims.claim: Direct human absolute/systemic availability measurements for lipophilic basic amines with aromatic rings and basic side chains—diphenhydramine (0.69), imipramine-N-oxide (~100%), urapidil (72–78%), donepezil (~100%), laquinimod (high), oxcarbazepine (89%), tiracizine (34%), moexipril (22%), and FK788 (55%)—support F ≥ 20% for the query.

L4 intestinal absorption/permeability records for close analogs show essentially complete absorption and high permeability: imipramine Fa ~100%, desipramine classified as intestinally absorbed and a high-permeability standard (Caco-2 Papp 82.8×10^-6 cm/s; MDCKII 38.3×10^-6 cm/s), and amitriptyline, pheniramine, and diphenhydramine show high Caco-2 permeability.

L5 gut-wall efflux records do not provide affirmative evidence for F < 20%: desipramine shows high permeability; imipramine has high Papp with efflux ratio ~1.1 in classic Caco-2 and remains highly permeable even with a FaSSIF efflux ratio of 2.0; amitriptyline shows no marked net efflux; methadone is a P-gp substrate yet P-gp inhibitors did not change its bioavailability; dexamphetamine shows efflux ratio 1.2; asimadoline shows ≥20% absorption within 1 h in both wild-type and P-gp knockout mice.

L6 hepatic clearance records show high intrinsic clearance for imipramine/desipramine in microsomes and hepatocytes, indicating first-pass metabolism, but they are not direct F outcomes; desipramine predicted hepatic clearance is moderate (6.4 mL/min/kg), and records show increased microsomal clearance did not change systemic availability (C263, C246), so this does not meet the affirmative low-F bar.

Low-F records for benazeprilat (<7%, dog 2.57%, cat 3.2%) and FK788 in rat (9.6%) come from polar acids/zwitterions or species-specific contexts and are not transferable to the lipophilic basic diamine query.

evidence_gaps: No direct absolute oral bioavailability measurement exists for the query molecule; all support is transferred from structurally related basic amines.
L3 oral AUC/Cmax records lack IV comparators, so they confirm exposure but not the F fraction.
L6 hepatic clearance data are for imipramine/desipramine, not the query; no query-specific metabolic stability or first-pass extraction fraction is available.
The query is predicted to be fully ionized (dicationic) at physiological pH; no direct permeability or efflux measurement quantifies the impact of the second positive charge.
No context exactly matches the N-phenyl-N-indanyl propylenediamine scaffold.
content.decision_summary: L6 hepatic clearance/metabolic-stability records for imipramine/desipramine show substantial first-pass metabolism, but they are not direct F outcomes and are partly mitigated by moderate predicted desipramine clearance and unchanged systemic availability despite increased clearance; combined with direct human F values for similar lipophilic basic amines and L4/L5 high absorption/low efflux evidence, F ≥ 20% remains better supported. Prediction remains high; confidence lowered to moderate.

every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
